query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of boron (around 0.1–0.3 at.%) during alloy processing can lead to its segregation at the internal boundaries of the dual-phase lamellar colonies, reducing microcrack initiation and simultaneously increasing strength through solute strengthening. This single intervention is expected to improve both the yield strength and room‐temperature ductility relative to the unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries that are prone to microcracking during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition of boron (approximately 0.1–0.3 at.%) during alloy synthesis/processing.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation tests. Process conditions should favor boron segregation to lamellar interfaces while avoiding the formation of brittle boride precipitates (e.g., using rapid solidification or suitable thermal treatments to promote interfacial segregation).
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at the interfaces between the lamellar phases, which enhances cohesion at these internal boundaries and reduces stress concentrators where microcracks could initiate.
generation.mechanism: The boron atoms preferentially partition to the internal lamellar boundaries, increasing boundary cohesion. This reduces the likelihood of microcrack initiation during tensile loading. At the same time, boron contributes to solid solution strengthening, thus potentially increasing yield strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy, the boron-doped alloy will demonstrate both increased tensile ductility (exhibiting a higher fracture strain) and enhanced yield strength at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies processed without boron addition, which shows limited tensile ductility and early microcrack-induced catastrophic failure at room temperature.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only within a narrow concentration range (~0.1–0.3 at.%). Exceeding this range may lead to the formation of brittle boride phases. Effectiveness also depends on processing conditions that ensure targeted segregation rather than random distribution.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal boron concentration and precise processing route to achieve targeted segregation without embrittlement are uncertain and require experimental optimization. The magnitude of improvement in strength and ductility remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the optimized boron addition (0.1–0.3 at.%) and one control set without boron. Use identical processing conditions tailored to promote interfacial boron segregation. Characterize the boron distribution at lamellar boundaries using atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM. Perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and fracture strain.
measurements: Tensile yield strength and fracture strain from mechanical testing
Microstructural characterization data confirming boron segregation at lamellar boundaries (via atom probe tomography or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile ductility and yield strength over the control samples, or if microstructural analysis reveals no preferential boron segregation at the lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis is rejected.
